papers.title: Reexamining the transcriptional landscape of plant specialized metabolism: from a hierarchical to a multi-layered and flatter regulatory model
papers.abstract: Abstract Plant specialized metabolites are essential mediators of adaptation to dynamic environmental conditions, functioning in defense, signaling, and developmental regulation. Traditionally, the regulation of plant specialized metabolism has been conceptualized through a hierarchical framework where global regulators dictate developmental cues which control downstream pathway-specific transcription factors (TFs) to activate individual biosynthetic pathways. In this model, primary metabolism is often considered a disconnected precursor supplier. Emerging genome-wide evidence has increasingly challenged this linear paradigm, revealing an underappreciated level of cross-talk and metabolic coordination. Regulatory networks exist on a quantitative spectrum from the linear hierarchical to highly decentralized flatter networks with extensive connections between both regulatory layers and input signals. This review synthesizes recent advances that suggest a shift in evidence indicating that a better regulatory model for specialized metabolism might be on the decentralized, "flatter" regulatory network architecture end of this spectrum. In this flatter model, individual TFs simultaneously target diverse promoter loci across multiple metabolic layers, while individual enzyme promoters are conversely targeted by a multitude of TFs. This integrated framework is exemplified by developing research spanning diverse classes of specialized metabolites, including glucosinolates, phenylpropanoids, and terpenoids. Focusing on these pathways, we discuss how flat TF networks simultaneously regulate precursor allocation, specialized metabolite production, and stress responsiveness, thereby linking primary and specialized metabolism into cohesive regulatory modules. Collectively, these findings suggest a shift from exclusively hierarchical models toward a flatter and distributed regulatory perspective that better reflects the precise signal-processing capacity and combinatorial control of plant metabolic regulation.

papers.title: Nutritional niches reveal mutualism resilience in urban fungus-farming ants
papers.abstract: Maintaining optimized nutrient exchange between partnered species across changing environments presents a fundamental challenge for nutritional mutualisms. Yet quantitative approaches linking nutrient acquisition by one partner with the nutritional requirements of the other have been lacking. Here we extend the Nutritional Geometry Framework from organisms and colonies to interspecific mutualisms by linking realized nutritional niches (RNNs) with nutritional performance landscapes to quantify nutritional homeostasis between interacting species. Nutritional analyses of thousands of DNA-barcoded plant fragments collected by free-ranging Panamanian leafcutter ants revealed that RNNs for fungal cultivar provisioning diverged between degraded urban and intact rainforest habitats. Despite this, colonies converged on similar nutritional intake targets that were similarly positioned relative to regions of high fungal performance, while fungal nutritional yield remained stable across habitats. These findings demonstrate that correspondence between colony nutritional intake and fungal nutritional performance provides a quantitative means of assessing nutritional homeostasis across interacting species and establishes a foundation for comparative analyses of nutrient exchange across mutualisms experiencing environmental change.

papers.title: Structural insights into inhibition and activation mechanisms of plant calcium-dependent protein kinases
papers.abstract: Calcium-dependent protein kinases (CDPKs) comprise the major group of Ca 2+ -regulated kinases in plants and protists. These enzymes comprise an N-terminal kinase domain and a C-terminal Ca 2+ -dependent activation domain (CAD). We solved the crystal structures of autoinhibited and activated forms of a plant CDPK, Arabidopsis CPK3. In the autoinhibited form, the CAD resembles a “dumbbell-like” calmodulin protein with a long helix in the N terminus that inhibits the kinase domain in a pseudo-substrate manner. Upon Ca 2+ binding to the four EF-hands, CAD undergoes a dramatic conformational change with a rotation around the kinase domain, thus exposing its active site for substrate recognition. Our structural and biochemical studies reveal that most plant CDPKs may involve distinct mechanisms of activation compared with CDPKs from the apicomplexan parasites.

papers.title: Competitive disruption of COI1 receptor assembly by a hemibiotrophic bacterial effector suppresses jasmonate-mediated immunity
papers.abstract: Hormone pathways are central hubs in plant immunity, and their receptors, the critical initiators of signaling cascades, are logical targets of pathogen effectors. The jasmonic acid (JA) pathway is a cornerstone of defense against phytopathogens, especially necrotrophs. However, whether pathogens can directly target its receptor COI1 to subvert this defense layer has remained unclear. Here, we show that JA signaling positively regulates resistance to the devastating hemibiotrophic pathogen Ralstonia solanacearum and identified a bacterial effector, RipBO, that directly targets COI1 to counteract this defense. RipBO binds with high affinity to the F-box domain of COI1, competitively disrupts the COI1-ASK interaction, and thereby blocks SCF COI1 complex assembly. This disruption effectively stabilizes JAZ repressors and paralyzes JA-mediated immunity. Our findings clarify the contribution of JA signaling to bacterial wilt resistance and identify direct targeting of the hormone receptor as a pathogen virulence strategy, pointing to a potential vulnerability for crop protection.

papers.title: Tandem duplication of oxidosqualene cyclases and enzyme promiscuity of cytochromes P450 contribute to the diversity of triterpenoids in Eleutherococcus senticosus
papers.abstract: Abstract Triterpenoid saponins in Araliaceae plants exhibit remarkable structural diversity, with species-specific compounds like ginsenosides and ciwujianosides, yet the genetic basis remains elusive. Here, we report a chromosome-scale genome assembly of Eleutherococcus senticosus (Rupr. & Maxim.) Maxim. (1.39 Gb, 51,243 genes) and demonstrate that it shares a lineage-specific whole-genome duplication (WGD-α, Ks = 0.112) with Hedera helix. Phylogenomic analyses reveal a 4:4 syntenic relationship between these species, confirming their close evolutionary relationship. Notably, both E. senticosus and H. helix lack the dammarenediol-II synthase (DDS) gene, explaining the absence of ginsenoside-type saponins. Through genome mining and functional validation, we identify eight OSC genes, including a tandemly duplicated cluster on chromosome 18 unique to E. senticosus. Biochemical assays show that EsOSC4 and EsOSC12 synthesize tirucalla-7,24-dien-3β-ol, representing the first enzymatic characterization of a tirucallane synthase in Araliaceae, while EsOSC13 produces lupeol. Site-directed mutagenesis establishes residue 372 (valine in EsOSC13, methionine in EsOSC4/12) as critical for this functional divergence. Moreover, we discover three promiscuous CYP716 enzymes (EsCYP716A244/A450/A452) capable of oxidizing β-amyrin, lupeol, and tirucalla-7,24-dien-3β-ol at multiple positions, generating diverse oxidized derivatives. These findings reveal tandem duplication and enzyme promiscuity as primary mechanisms driving triterpenoid diversity in E. senticosus, with implications for synthetic biology applications in saponin production.

H3.1K27me1-mediated regulation of TONSOKU is required for viability in plants
papers.abstract: Abstract Histone H3.1 lysine 27 monomethylation (H3.1K27me1), catalyzed in plants by the SET domain proteins ATXR5 and ATXR6 (ATXR5/6), has been implicated in transposon silencing, stress-response gene repression, chromatin organization, epigenetic inheritance, and genome stability. However, functional analyses have been limited by the lethality of atxr5/6 loss-of-function mutants, necessitating the use of hypomorphic alleles that retain residual ATXR6 activity. Here, we show that the inviability of atxr5/6 null mutants (atxr5/6null) depends entirely on the DNA repair protein TONSOKU (TSK). Disruption of TSK activity enables the recovery of viable plants lacking ATXR5/6-dependent H3.1K27me1. To uncouple the consequences of H3.1K27me1 loss from defects associated with strong tsk mutants, we generated a hypomorphic tsk allele (tsk1-616) that maintains near-normal development and genomic stability. Using atxr5/6null tsk1-616 plants, we find that complete loss of ATXR5/6-dependent H3.1K27me1 has no effect on H3K27me3 at the genome-wide level, whereas H3K9me2 and CHG methylation are modestly increased. Transposon activation, stress-induced gene expression, heterochromatin amplification, and developmental defects previously observed in hypomorphic atxr5/6 mutants are mostly suppressed in atxr5/6null tsk1-616 plants. In contrast, chromocenter decondensation persists, suggesting a direct role for H3.1K27me1 in higher-order chromatin organization. Overall, these findings indicate that H3.1K27me1 primarily functions as a post-replicative chromatin maturation mark that restricts TSK activity to maintain genome stability.

A transcriptomic atlas of grass senescence reveals divergent underground sink networks promote nitrogen recycling in perennials
papers.abstract: Abstract Senescence enables plants to remobilize and recycle nutrients from aging organs to support growth, reproduction, and survival. In annual crops like maize, nitrogen remobilization from leaves to grain is incomplete, with 30-50% of nitrogen remaining in crop residue where it may be subject to environmental loss. Mitigating nitrogen loss in annual crops could be achieved by leveraging the physiological strategies of perennial grasses, which remobilize nitrogen and other nutrients into underground organs at the end of the growing season, thereby preventing environmental leakage. To uncover the molecular basis of perennial nitrogen recycling to underground organs, we built a transcriptomic atlas from field-grown plants, comprising 2,685 RNA-seq libraries from 14 grass species within the Panicoideae (Poaceae), utilizing maize and sorghum as annual references for comparative analyses. The atlas spans leaves, roots, stalks, and rhizomes across two seasons, from mid-growing season to senescence. Using a photosynthetic index to align the leaf’s transition from nitrogen sink to source across species, co-expression network analysis revealed that the subnetworks driving leaf nitrogen remobilization are preserved across annuals and perennials. However, we discovered that the subnetworks associated with underground sink establishment, specifically those associated with seed-like dormancy and desiccation tolerance pathways, have diverged among annual crop accessions. Our work identifies conserved gene candidates and networks that could reintroduce perennial-like nutrient recycling into annual crops to enhance long-term nutrient retention in the field.

papers.title: Transcriptional regulatory landscape of plum ( Prunus salicina ) fruit ripening
papers.abstract: Abstract Fruit ripening in plum (Prunus salicina) involves a complex transcriptional regulatory network, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study presents a comprehensive transcriptional regulatory landscape of plum fruit ripening by integrating multi-omics data, including transcriptome, chromatin accessibility (DNase-seq), and DNA affinity purification sequencing (DAP-seq) of multiple ripening responsive transcription factors (TFs) from EIL, NAC, bZIP, WRKY, MYB, and C2H2 families. We constructed a position-resolved regulatory network, revealing the dynamic modulation of multiple ripening processes, especially sugar accumulation. The key ethylene signaling TF PsEIN3-1 directly binds to the promoters of PsbZIP44 and PsNAC1, which in turn, further bind to key enzyme genes involved in ethylene biosynthesis, starch degradation, and sugar accumulation. The regulatory effects of PsbZIP44 on plum fruit ripening and sugar accumulation were preliminarily verified through transient transformation experiments. Through comparative analysis with other Prunus species (plum, peach, apricot, and sweet cherry), we uncovered both conserved regulatory circuits governing ripening. Additionally, we developed the Prunus Regulome Atlas http://plantencode.fun/regulome/prunus/that hosts multiple omics data and interactive regulatory networks of Prunus. Our findings provide novel insights into the transcriptional regulation of plum fruit ripening and serve as a foundational resource for future functional studies and breeding improvement in Prunus species.

papers.title: Rhizospheric pH mediated thermo-signalling coordinates root growth under heat stress
papers.abstract: Abstract Heat stress events pose a major threat to global agriculture due to elevated air and soil temperatures. While plant roots regulate their growth in response to elevated soil temperatures, they appear to rely on thermosensory mechanisms distinct from those used by shoots. Here, we report pH as a key component of a thermo-signaling mechanism that regulates temperature-dependent root responses via ROS-mediated control of cell cycle dynamics in Arabidopsis thaliana . At moderately high temperatures, alkalization of meristematic and transition zones increases superoxide (O₂⁻) levels, promoting cell division and root growth. Conversely, higher temperatures inhibit growth by increasing acidification and hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) accumulation in these zones. Elevating external pH buffers this acidification, reduces H₂O₂ levels, and confers heat resistance. Our data support that this pH-mediated heat resistance is also effective under soil conditions. The heat-induced pH shifts are controlled by plasma membrane H⁺-ATPases (PM-H⁺-ATPases), which are under the control of the kinases TOT3 and TOI5. Our findings reveal an interesting pathway for plant adaptation to heat stress, linking pH, ROS and root thermomorphogenesis, with major implications for improving plant resilience in warming climates.

OsMED25-OsWRI1 Fine-Tunes Fatty Acid Biosynthesis: A Key Strategy via Intron Retention
papers.abstract: Abstract In rice grains, the mechanisms governing fatty acid biosynthesis remain largely elusive. Although WRINKLED1 (WRI1) is well established as a core transcription factor activating fatty acid biosynthesis under multi-level regulation, its post-transcriptional regulation has been scarcely explored. Here, we demonstrate that OsWRI1 transcripts undergo alternative splicing (AS) via intron retention (IR), producing two functionally distinct splice variants: OsWRI1α and OsWRI1β. OsWRI1α encodes a canonical protein containing two AP2 domains, whereas OsWRI1β produces a truncated protein due to a premature termination codon. Genetic analyses confirm that OsWRI1α functions as a positive regulator of fatty acid biosynthesis, while OsWRI1β exerts an inhibitory effect by directly interacting with OsWRI1α, disrupting its dimerization, and preventing activation of downstream target genes including OsACP1 and OsFAD2. We further identify OsMED25 as a critical regulator of this AS event. OsMED25 is recruited to a 360-bp intronic region of OsWRI1 that corresponds precisely to the retained intron in OsWRI1β, where it recruits the splicing factor OsPTB4 to promote intron retention, thereby repressing fatty acid biosynthesis. The induction of OsWRI1β expression by jasmonic acid (JA) signaling, which we identify as a suppressor of fatty acid biosynthesis, is strictly dependent on OsMED25. Mechanistically, JA enhances OsMED25 protein stability and promotes its association with OsWRI1 pre-mRNA. Together, these findings establish that IR-mediated AS of OsWRI1 defines a regulatory mechanism where the JA-OsMED25-OsPTB4-OsWRI1 axis coordinates carbon flux and energy homeostasis during grain lipid accumulation. Thus, OsMED25 integrates upstream JA signaling to fine-tune OsWRI1 splicing, modulating fatty acid biosynthesis during rice grain development.

papers.title: Phototropin-mediated blue light signaling orients the asymmetry of Marchantia polymorpha spores
papers.abstract: Multicellular organisms produced by sexual reproduction develop from single cells, and the asymmetry of these cells can define the orientation of the earliest developmental axes. The haploid multicellular stage of the plant, Marchantia polymorpha, develops from a single cell—the spore—that divides asymmetrically, producing an apical germ cell that generates the plant body and a smaller basal cell that differentiates as an anchoring germ rhizoid cell. We show that the orientation of this asymmetric cell division is controlled by an external environmental cue—blue light—that is perceived by the photoreceptor phototropin. This process requires the NCH1 (NRL PROTEIN FOR CHLOROPLAST MOVEMENT 1) protein for downstream signaling. Together, these findings define core elements of the mechanism by which a directional environmental signal orients cell division, which, in turn, orients the first axis of symmetry.

papers.title: Developmental Rewiring of a Brassinosteroid Signaling Module Controls Anther Patterning and Tapetum Specification in Arabidopsis
papers.abstract: Abstract Male reproductive development in plants relies on the precise patterning of anther locules and the specification of the tapetum layer. While the BRASSINAZOLE RESISTANT (BZR) family transcription factors are essential for both processes, they function independently of the brassinosteroid (BR) receptors, leaving their upstream signaling mechanism unknown. Here, through systematic genetic analysis, we show that a core BR-signaling module, comprising BR-SIGNALING KINASEs (BSKs) and BRASSINOSTEROID-INSENSITIVE 2 (BIN2), is repurposed downstream of the tapetum regulator the receptor kinase EXCESS MICROSPOROCYTES1 (EMS1) and functions upstream of BZRs. Within this reconfigured pathway, EMS1 recruits BSKs, which in turn inactivate BIN2, thereby releasing BZRs in a conserved hierarchy cascade mirroring BR signaling to drive tapetum specification. Additionally, this BSKs-BIN2-BZRs signaling module also functions in anther locule formation. Conversely, BSU1-LIKE2/3 (BSL2/3), homologs of the positive BR regulator BSU1, act as repressors in this context. This pathway transcriptionally activates the cyclins such as CYCB1;1 to initiate tapetal cell division, while BSL2/3 ensure its timely termination by promoting CYCB1;1 protein degradation. Our work defines the signaling framework governing anther development and establishes a paradigm in which conserved signaling components are rewired to achieve developmental specificity.

papers.title: ABI1/ABI2-mediated dephosphorylation of NRAMP1 couples ABA signaling to manganese homeostasis
papers.abstract: Abstract Manganese (Mn) homeostasis, the precise regulation of cellular Mn levels, is crucial for plant growth and is maintained primarily through the transporter NATURAL RESISTANCE-ASSOCIATED MACROPHAGE PROTEIN 1 (NRAMP1). While the kinases responsible for its phosphorylation are well-established, the phosphatases mediating its dephosphorylation remain unidentified. We identify ABI1 and ABI2 as the phosphatases acting on NRAMP1, linking ABA signaling to Mn homeostasis. Mn stresses trigger ABA to inhibit ABI1/2, which may enable NRAMP1 phosphorylation and stress initiation. A feedback loop then appears to induce short-term ABI1/2 reactivation, mediating site-specific dephosphorylation of NRAMP1 at Thr498 (to fine-tune uptake under deficiency) and at Ser20 (to limit endocytosis under toxicity). This dephosphorylation restrains overactivation and contributes to the maintenance of Mn ion balance. Subsequent ABI1/2 attenuation may facilitates long-term adaptation. Collectively, our findings support the ABA-ABI1/2-NRAMP1 axis as a feedback-regulated circuit controlling Mn homeostasis; this work reveals an expanded functional repertoire for ABA-signaling PP2Cs and identifies a targetable module for enhancing crop resilience to Mn stress.

papers.title: The ZmJAZ14–ZmMYC2 module regulates anthesis–silking synchrony in maize
papers.abstract: The evolution of traits can increase yield potential but may create physiological constraints. Jasmonic acid (JA) signaling regulates sex determination in male (tassel) and female (ear) inflorescences in maize. Although the formation of ears laid the foundation for high yields, the asynchronous development of the tassel and the ear prolongs the anthesis-silking interval (ASI), threatening reproductive success and reducing yield. Whether JA signaling coordinates ear and tassel development remains unclear. Here, we show that the core JA signaling module, ZmJAZ14-ZmMYC2a/b, orchestrates the expression of SPL29 for reproductive transition, BA1 for female inflorescence initiation, and EXPA5 for silk elongation. Coordination of these physiological processes underpins synchronous growth of the tassel and ears, whereas disruption of ZmMYC2a/b or accumulation of the repressor ZmJAZ14 prolongs ASI. Our work suggests that the repurposing of JA signaling to coordinate ear and tassel development may represent a lineage-specific evolutionary burden in maize. Deciphering the link between gains and unforeseen costs of evolution could further improve yields.

papers.title: The transcription factors OsIDD and OsSHR jointly regulate ground tissue patterning and differentiation in rice roots
papers.abstract: Rice roots have a distinctive ground tissue architecture with multiple cortical layers and a single endodermal layer concentrically surrounding the stele. This architecture promotes aerenchyma formation and adaptability to waterlogged environments, but the underlying molecular mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here, we identified the INDETERMINATE DOMAIN (IDD) and SHORTROOT (SHR) families as key regulators of ground tissue development in rice. OsIDD2/3/6/8 govern cortical radial symmetry by coordinating cortical organization and auxin distribution independently of OsSHR1/2/3/4/5. Quadruple knockout of OsIDD2/3/6/8 caused cortical asymmetry without affecting apoplastic barrier integrity or mineral uptake but reduced shoot-directed ion transport. OsIDD8 also controls the number of cortical cell layers and endodermal cells, whereas OsSHR1/2/3/4/5 redundantly promote periclinal divisions of the cortical cells, which require OsIDD8 activity. Moreover, OsIDD and OsSHR members coordinate endodermal differentiation by regulating localization of Casparian strip membrane domain protein OsCASP1 and lignin/suberin deposition. These findings establish a genetic framework underlying the spatial organization and functional differentiation of ground tissue in rice roots.

papers.title: HDAC1/2 mediates the chloroplast unfolded protein response through histone H4 deacetylation in Chlamydomonas
papers.abstract: Abstract Disruption of chloroplast proteostasis activates retrograde signaling that reprograms nuclear gene expression. However, how these signals are integrated with chromatin-based transcriptional regulation remains poorly understood. Here, using a genetic suppressor screen of a conditional ClpP1-depletion mutant, we identified a histone deacetylase HDAC1/2 as a regulator of chloroplast stress signaling in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii. Loss of HDAC1/2 alleviated growth inhibition and reduced cell death caused by disruption of chloroplast proteostasis following ClpP1 depletion. Furthermore, HDAC1/2 deficiency enhanced tolerance to high-light, oxidative, and endoplasmic reticulum stresses, as well as chloroplast translation inhibition. These stress conditions increased H2O2 levels and HDAC1/2 protein accumulation, suggesting that H2O2 may act as a common upstream signal. Additionally, HDAC1/2 deficiency also disrupted the transcriptional response to ClpP1 depletion, particularly affecting genes involved in photosynthesis, redox homeostasis, DNA metabolism, cell-cycle regulation, and ROS scavenging. This altered response was accompanied by increased histone H4 acetylation. Together, our findings identify HDAC1/2 as an important regulator connecting organellar proteostasis signaling with nuclear epigenetic regulation and suggest a role for H2O2 associated chromatin remodeling in coordinating cellular stress responses.

Latitude modulates climate-driven maize yield gains across the central U.S. “warming hole”
papers.abstract: Abstract Maize yield responses to climate change differ seasonally and regionally, with both positive and negative impacts shaped by local climate trends and management decisions. Here, using a phenology-aligned moving crop-season framework and the Hybrid-Maize model (1991–2024) across five U.S. Corn Belt states, we quantify climate-driven yield contributions and show that they transition from southern declines to northern gains, reflecting the persistent influence of the central U.S. summer warming hole characterized by cooling maximum temperatures and increasing rainfall. A systematic thermal mismatch between environmental heat availability and hybrid growing degree day requirements is observed, particularly south of 42°N, where thermal matching declined despite favorable thermal conditions. Contrasting trends in thermal matching and reproductive duration help explain the latitude-dependent structure of climate-driven yield contributions. Our findings highlight how hybrid selection modulates the impacts of temperature, precipitation, vapor pressure deficit, and radiation trends on maize yield gains across the U.S. Corn Belt.

papers.title: Cell lineages of soybean anther morphogenesis reveal developmental trajectory of microsporocytes at single-cell resolution
papers.abstract: Abstract In flowering plants, anther morphogenesis and microspore mother cell (MMC) specification of the male reproductive organ are critical for fertility and seed-setting or yield, but their underlying mechanisms in soybean (Glycine max) remain largely uncharacterized. Here, we cytologically established a staged developmental framework of early soybean anthers that were collected to generate a high-resolution single-nucleus RNA-seq atlas. We further characterized 11 major cell types annotated by cluster-specific marker genes and validated by RNA in situ hybridization. Pseudotime trajectory analysis reconstructed the differentiation process of microsporocytes, tapetum, and middle layer from archesporial cells, and established a regulatory network governing germline development. Parallel comparison of mitotic dividing cells (DCs) and meiotic MMCs revealed divergent transcriptional and cell-cycle programs. DCs follow a linear mitotic cascade with smooth, continuous transcriptional regulation, whereas MMCs undergo lineage-specific transcriptional reprogramming with an oscillatory activation of cell-cycle regulators to orchestrate meiotic transitions and progression. By comparing the transcriptional regulatory network of DCs and MMCs, we identified a pair of C2H2 zinc finger factors GmKNUa/b, the homologs of Arabidopsis KNUCKLES, as a key switch for MMC differentiation in soybean. The CRISPR-Cas9-edited Gmknua/b double mutants lack meiocytes, and GmKNUa/b might trigger the mitosis-to-meiosis transition by repressing the persistent mitotic cell cycle. Taken together, these results reveal the cellular signatures and molecular basis of early soybean anther morphogenesis and germline specialization, and provide candidate targets for manipulating germline fate and male fertility in soybean.

papers.title: PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 7 moderates the activity of phytochrome A in persistent canopy shade conditions
papers.abstract: In nature, plants perceive and respond to complex vegetative environments through the phytochrome (phy) photoreceptor-signaling system. The Canopy Adaptation Strategy, elicited by phyA, together with the Shade Avoidance Syndrome, regulated by phyB, enables plants to adapt to diverse forms of vegetation shade. The phyA High Irradiance Response mode, which involves photocycle-coupled nuclear shuttling, is essential for sensing sustained far-red-rich conditions typical of canopy or occlusive shade. Our research identifies PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 7 (PIF7) as a key regulator of phyA function. We show that PIF7 overexpression (PIF7ox) effectively suppresses phyA action. Under persistent shade, PIF7 and phyA both accumulate and associate within nuclear photobodies, with this interaction mediated by the C-terminal domain of PIF7 and the PAS-PAS domain of phyA. PIF7 also interacts with FAR-RED ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL 1 (FHY1) and FHY1-LIKE transport facilitators, thereby interfering with phyA cytosolic-nuclear shuttling. This coordinated molecular targeting by PIF7 constitutes an effective strategy for modulating phyA function under persistent shade conditions.
papers.affiliation: Institute of Molecular Plant Sciences, School of Biological Sciences, University of Edinburgh
